props.title: Tous les garçons s'appellent Patrick
props.initialSlug: Two sisters unknowingly date the same charming flirt

sections.content: Jean-Luc Godard's early short film **Tous les garçons s'appellent Patrick** (1959) marks a crucial stepping stone between his film criticism years and his groundbreaking feature **Breathless** (1960). Written by Eric Rohmer, this 21-minute comedy perfectly encapsulates the playful spirit that would define the French New Wave. The story of two female roommates unknowingly dating the same smooth-talking player named Patrick showcases Godard's early experimentation with jump cuts, street photography, and naturalistic performances that would revolutionize cinema.

sections.content: The film's innovative street shooting style directly influenced the guerrilla filmmaking techniques of **Band of Outsiders** (1964) and **Masculin Féminin** (1966). Cinematographer Michel Latouche's nimble camera movement through Paris streets established the documentary-like approach that became a hallmark of New Wave cinema. The natural lighting and real locations represented a decisive break from the artificial studio system, paralleling similar innovations in **The 400 Blows** (1959) by François Truffaut.

The playful treatment of romantic relationships and modern youth culture anticipates later New Wave classics like **Une femme est une femme** (1961) and Rohmer's own **My Night at Maud's** (1969). The film's clever structure, following the same events from different perspectives, demonstrates the kind of formal experimentation that would become more radical in works like **Last Year at Marienbad** (1961) and **Cléo from 5 to 7** (1962). sections.content: While brief, **Tous les garçons s'appellent Patrick** contains many elements that would become New Wave signatures: direct address to camera, location shooting, jump cuts, and contemporary youth culture. The film's exploration of modern relationships influenced later works like **La Collectionneuse** (1967) and **Love in the Afternoon** (1972), establishing themes that directors would explore throughout the 1960s and beyond.
